title: 41.5 percent of surveyed Japanese middle schoolers don’t think more immigration benefits society
description: This isn’t a cut-and-dry case of Japanese kids simply becoming more socially conservative, though. Internationalism is becoming an increasingly discussed topic in Japan, as the country’s indigenous population contracts and its number of foreign-national residents increases. This shift is happening quickly enough to be noticed not only by adults comparing the current demographics to how […]
content:
This isn’t a cut-and-dry case of Japanese kids simply becoming more socially conservative, though.

Internationalism is becoming an increasingly discussed topic in Japan, as the country’s indigenous population contracts and its number of foreign-national residents increases. This shift is happening quickly enough to be noticed not only by adults comparing the current demographics to how they were decades ago, but by adolescents too, and a recent study shows that many of them don’t necessarily see Japan’s growing foreign population as a good thing.

University of Tokyo sociology professor Norihiro Nihei conducts a periodic survey of all students at 10 middle schools in Tokyo and the surrounding area in order to track changes in their attitudes regarding social issues. The students are presented with a series of statements, then asked whether they agree or disagree with them. One of those statements is “An increase in the number of foreigners living in Japan will bring many benefits to society,” and in the most recent survey, more than 40 percent said they do not agree.

An increase in the number of foreigners living in Japan will bring many benefits to society
● Do not agree at all: 9.6 percent of respondents
● Somewhat disagree: 31.9 percent
● Somewhat agree: 39.8 percent
● Strongly agree: 18.6 percent

The percentage of students disagreeing with the notion that immigration would be beneficial to Japanese society nearly doubled between the most recent survey, the data for which was collected in 2025, and the previous iteration of the survey, which was carried out in 2023.

An increase in the number of foreigners living in Japan will bring many benefits to society (2023 results)
● Do not agree at all: 3.96 percent of respondents
● Somewhat disagree: 18.3 percent
● Somewhat agree: 50.4 percent
● Strongly agree: 27.4 percent

That jump from 22.26 percent who didn’t see increasing immigration as a major positive for society in 2023 to 41.5 percent in 2025 is significant. Nihei is quick to say, though, that this doesn’t signal an across-the-board shift towards right-wing attitudes for young people in Japan. As a matter of fact, he asserts that the way the labels “liberal” and “conservative” are used in Japan and the English-speaking world don’t always perfectly align, and so he wants to put a finer point on how the survey is applying the terms.

For the purposes of the survey, Nihei examines what he describes as three indicators of liberal orientation: democratic orientation, tolerance, and autonomous orientation, which the study checks for by presenting a statement representing each. Among them, there were no dramatic drops since the previous survey.

Total percentage of agree/strongly agree responses for:
● Rules should be decided through everyone’s discussion. (democratic orientation)
2025: 96 percent
2023: 95.1 percent
● I can accept people with different ways of thinking. (tolerance)
2025: 91.6 percent
2023: 92.1 percent
● It is important to stay true to oneself in any situation. (autonomous orientation)
2025: 83 percent
2023: 87.1 percent

There were, however, some large increases in agreement to statements that, within the scope of the study, Nihei cites as indicators of conservative or right-wing orientations of authoritarianism, patriotism, and xenophobia.

Total percentage of agree/strongly agree responses for:
● I should follow the instructions of teachers and seniors rather than my own thoughts. (authoritarianism)
2025: 61.3 percent
2023: 57.4 percent
● It is important to love one’s country. (patriotism)
2025: 86.8 percent
2023: 76.9 percent

Total percentage of disagree/strongly disagree responses for:
● An increase in the number of foreigners living in Japan will bring many benefits to society. (xenophobia-related attitudes)
2025: 41.5 percent
2023: 23.1 percent

It might seem like an odd combination to have continuing extremely high-expressed support for accepting other people’s way of thinking and collectively deciding on the rules while at the same time having a jump in uncertainty as to whether or not more foreigners living in Japan is a good thing for society, but there’s one other factor the survey examines, which Nihei calls “rule strictness,” measured by the participant’s reactions to the statement “People who do not follow rules should be severely punished,” which 70.8 percent of respondents agreed with in 2022. In 2025, the percentage rose to 79.3 percent.

The idea of strict enforcement of regulations might seem like something from the conservative school of thought, and Nihei does recognize that such strictness could be seen as the opposite of tolerance, which he treats as a liberal value. However, in an example of one of the many ways conservative and social values may not consist of the same baskets of attitudes in one society as they do in another, Nihei says:

“This concept sits on a different axis from the liberal/conservative spectrum. Literally standing at the opposite pole of tolerance, it appears non-liberal on the surface. On the other hand, rule compliance has historically served as a prerequisite for managing a fair society by restraining arbitrary uses of power, thus forming an essential element of liberalism. This is also linked to constitutionalism, having played a key role for the left as well in various forms, such as refusing to tolerate ‘slush-fund lawmakers.’”

Taken together, the combination of, to borrow the survey’s terminology, continuing high tolerance at the same time that both xenophobia and rule strictness are increasing could be construed as reflecting a change in Japanese young people’s perception as to how willing foreigners are to follow Japan’s laws and social customs. Though Nihei’s report on the most recent survey’s results don’t delve into this issue, high-profile crimes such as theft and assault involving foreign perpetrators used to be few and far between, but have become not-uncommon occurrences in recent years, and could be contributing to a diminished image of foreign residents’ likelihood of integrating into the peaceful, orderly norms that have long been the default for most Japanese communities. That sort of stigma could be especially influential on Japanese children, who might not have any foreigners among their peers, as Japan’s foreign population has far more adults than minors, and so might not have any personal acquaintances to counteract the bad examples that become major news stories.

The survey being conducted in the Tokyo area could also be affecting the results, as one of the most commonly pointed-to concrete ways in which Japan could benefit from increased immigration is help in filling labor shortages and preventing population vacuums in smaller communities whose Japanese residents are moving to the big cities, but those aren’t problems that Tokyo and its immediate neighbors are really struggling with. The current state of the economy is also a likely factor in the growing skepticism about immigration among the surveyed middle schoolers. Proponents of increased immigration within the Japanese government have been advocating for expanded support for foreign residents to promote smoother integration into Japanese society. Unfortunately, this is occurring at the same time that rapidly rising costs of living and stagnant wages are putting the pinch on Japan’s middle and lower classes. Middle schoolers probably aren’t tracking consumer price indexes and sifting through government budget proposals, but many probably do have a sense that money is getting tighter for their or their classmates’ families, and so the idea of an increased focus on helping foreign residents coinciding with a decrease in their perceived willingness to follow the rules might not sit well with many of the survey participants.

It’s very important, though, to keep in mind that 41.5 percent of the surveyed middle schoolers saying they don’t think an increase in foreign residents will be beneficial to society also means that 58.5 percent of them, the majority, do think that increased immigration would be a good thing. In other words, xenophobia isn’t the default attitude among Japanese kids, and hopefully whatever factors are contributing to the bump of the needle in that direction can be resolved while that’s still the case.

Source: Kyodo via Jin, Japan Policy Forum

title: Tokyo neighborhood adds new “smart trash cans” to deal with increasing amounts of tourist litter
description: A high-tech part of Tokyo gets some high-tech help in addressing an overtourism problem and responding to a common traveler complaint. Downtown Tokyo’s Akihabara neighborhood is already one of the most popular tourism destinations for travelers in Japan, by nature of being the country’s center of anime and video game fan culture, and a couple […]
content:
A high-tech part of Tokyo gets some high-tech help in addressing an overtourism problem and responding to a common traveler complaint.

Downtown Tokyo’s Akihabara neighborhood is already one of the most popular tourism destinations for travelers in Japan, by nature of being the country’s center of anime and video game fan culture, and a couple of new additions to the district are sure to be instant crowd pleasers too. We’re not talking about a new multi-level arcade or manga merch specialty store, though, but a bunch of new public trash cans.

Japan’s relative lack of trash receptacles in public spaces has long been among the top complaint from foreign visitors to the country, and it’s an issue that exists even in the most densely developed parts of Tokyo. In recent years, there’s been a noticeable increase in the amount of litter to be seen in the city’s most heavily touristed areas, including Akihabara.

▼ A pile of trash on the sidewalk in Akihabara in January of this year

Using funds from the municipal government’s Tokyo Green Up Action subsidy program, Chiyoda Ward, which Akihabara is part of, has acquired 22 SmaGO “smart trash cans” from Tokyo-based tech company Forcetec. Fittingly for Akihabara’s image as a high-tech part of town, these receptacles are actually public trash compactors, using solar power to condense their contents down to one-fifth of their original size. They can also utilize a cloud network to inform maintenance workers of how full the bins currently are, allowing for more efficient coordination of trash pickups.

▼ As is usually the case in Japan, different types of trash go in different containers, so make sure to sort your stuff before you toss it in.

The SmaGO trash cans went into service at 10 locations in Akihabara, clustered around Akihabara Station (秋葉原駅 in the map below) and along Chuo-dori (中央通り), the major shopping street in the neighborhood.

The move follows new ordinances requiring more publicly accessible trash cans, and stricter penalties for not using them, which recently went into effect across town in the Shibuya neighborhood. Both districts’ responses to increasing amounts of litter do make one feel a little sad that the current crop of visitors evidently isn’t as concerned with Japan’s customary etiquette norm of carrying your trash home with you if there’s no public place to dispose of it, but hopefully the new initiatives will result in a return to cleaner streets.

title: Why people in Japan hardly ever say “sayonara,” and what they say instead
description: Everyone knows that sayonara means goodbye in Japanese, but goodbye in Japan doesn’t always mean you need to say it. You don’t have to be an anime otaku, foodie with a penchant for matcha and wagyu, or obsessive linguistics enthusiast that know that sayonara means “goodbye” in Japanese. Like loco in Spanish and merci in French, […]
content:
Everyone knows that sayonara means goodbye in Japanese, but goodbye in Japan doesn’t always mean you need to say it.

You don’t have to be an anime otaku, foodie with a penchant for matcha and wagyu, or obsessive linguistics enthusiast that know that sayonara means “goodbye” in Japanese. Like loco in Spanish and merci in French, sayonara is one of those words that’s so well known internationally that it’s widely understood even by people without any personal connection to its home-country culture.

And yet, living in Japan, you’ll very rarely hear anyone actually say sayonara (unless you happen to be in a pre-college school, where students of such ages say it to their teachers at the end of the school day). As a matter of fact, when someone did say it to us the other day, it was startling, even if it was also very appropriate to the specific circumstances that was taking place.

But wait, if sayonara isn’t a commonly used phrase, how do people in Japan end conversations? Does one person just wander off once they think the topic has run its course, and the value that Japanese culture places on tacit understanding means that you’re just supposed to infer that the other person said goodbye to you inside their heart?

▼ Wait, Linguistics Samurai! I still had something I needed to tell you!

Nope. Japanese actually has several other phrases that take sayonara’s place in the vast majority of daily situations. Let’s take a look at a few, and then circle back to why sayonara usually isn’t used.

One of the most common ways to say goodbye when speaking to friends or peers in social situations is ja, which means “if” or “then.” That might seem like a pretty random choice of vocabulary, but there is a logical reason for it, which is that it’s a shortened version of sore ja, meaning “if it’s like that,” or, rendered more naturally in English “in that case” or “well then.”

In this situation, sore ja is itself a pared-down version of phrases such as sore ja, kore de kaerimasu (“well then, I’m heading home”), sore ja, ikanakya” (“well then, I’ve got to get going”), and the like. But if you don’t want to get into the nitty-gritty of why you’re saying goodbye, Japanese social norms allow you to opt out of the explanation and just say “ja.” Used completely by itself, though, ja can sound a little curt, so to make it a little cordial the all-purpose emphasizer ne, or na among male speakers, is often tacked onto the end.

Speaking of adding things after ja, another option for that is mata, the Japanese word for “again.” In this case, it’s included as an abbreviation of things such as mata aimashou (“let’s get together again [sometime]”) or mata ashita (“[see you] again tomorrow”). And to multiply our options even further, if you want to sound a little more polished and polite, you can replace ja with dewa, a more formal word with the same meaning.

Mixing and matching these elements will give you all sorts of common ways of saying “goodbye” in Japanese that you’ll hear much, much more frequently than sayonara, such as:
● ja / ja ne / ja na
● dewa
● sore ja / sore dewa
● mata / mata ne / mata na
● sore ja, mata / sore ja, mata ne / sore ja, mata na
● dewa, mata ne / dewa, mata na

There are two other Japanese phrases which also don’t translate literally as “goodbye” but regularly get used where we’d say that in English. One of them is otsukarasama desu, which, as we’ve discussed before, more or less means “you must be tired,” but which is commonly said between coworkers when going home at the end of the day, since you’ve both put in a full day of work. Similarly, if you’re going home while someone else is still working, the custom is to tell them osaki ni shitsurei shimasu, meaning “excuse me for going home before you,” which can be shortened down to just osaki ni if you’re on friendly terms with one another.

But even knowing all that, sayonara does still mean “goodbye,” so why isn’t it said very often? Because sayonara has a very weighty nuance to it, so much so that it’s mainly used for situations where it’s not just goodbye, but possibly goodbye forever, or at the very least where there’s a very real possibility that you’ll never meet again.

▼ Hearing “sayonara” at the end of a first date is a strong sign that there’s not going to be a second.

Because of that, sayonara isn’t something classmates say to each other after grabbing ramen together. It’s what they might say to each other at graduation if they’re all going off to different colleges and there’s no real guarantee they’re going to meet up again. You wouldn’t say sayonara to your coworker Tanaka-san when you clock out on a Friday evening, but you might say it to him at his going away party before his permanent transfer to an overseas office.

▼ If your coworker walks out of the office while waving and saying “Sayonara!”, there’s a good chance she just quit.

In other words, when someone does tell you sayonara, it tends to stick with you, because it’s a sign of parting that might be permanent. When someone said it to us the other day, it was a bittersweet moment, so who did we hear it from?

The workers at Cold Stone in the city of Kamakura, the very last branch of the chain in all of east Japan, which we visited for one last ice cream treat shortly before it closed on October 31.

While he was waiting for his order, our reporter Mr. Sato briefly chatted with the staff about the shop shutting down, and when they handed him his ice cream, they told him thank you, and also “sayonara.” This is Cold Stone’s second time to leave east Japan, and it wouldn’t be a shock if the company decides not to ever take a third shot at it, and that situation was reflected in the employees’ choice of words.

Now, none of this means that there’s a taboo against saying sayonara, or that it’s an old-fashioned phrase that feels out of place in the modern world. Sayonara does, though, carry a lot of emotional significance, so it’s a special phrase for special circumstances.

title: Tokyo cracks down on Airbnb-style rentals with new laws limiting operator days and more
description: With tourists’ and residents’ feelings about minpaku racing in opposite directions, wards add new local ordinances onto national laws. “Short-term private vacation lodging” is a bit of a mouthful, and while “Airbnb-style rentals” is more concise, it singles out just one company in what’s become a rapidly expanding sector of traveler accommodations. So today, let’s […]
content:
With tourists’ and residents’ feelings about minpaku racing in opposite directions, wards add new local ordinances onto national laws.

“Short-term private vacation lodging” is a bit of a mouthful, and while “Airbnb-style rentals” is more concise, it singles out just one company in what’s become a rapidly expanding sector of traveler accommodations. So today, let’s just call them “minpaku,” the term used in Japanese to describe rentals for travelers that weren’t originally zoned or constructed as hotels.

Minpaku have been rapidly rising in popularity over the past few years. While the idea of staying in a converted home while on vacation has limited appeal to most Japanese travelers, foreign tourists have shown plenty of enthusiasm for minpaku, especially when coming to Japan in a group of friends or family members who want more communal space for their party than conventional hotels offer. That growing popularity with foreign tourists has simultaneously made minpaku’s presence increasingly unwelcome among local Japanese residents, however, and new ordinances mean that all 23 central wards of Tokyo have now introduced additional rules restricting or limiting their operation, including new bans on accepting guests on weekdays.

Houses and apartments are built very close to one another in Japan’s residential neighborhoods. and that creates a sort of etiquette-deterrence situation between long-term residents. The close proximity means that any excess noise or trash generated by one neighbor is likely to affect everyone around them, and vice versa, so residents generally try to stay quiet and clean as a show of mutual consideration, with the baseline tacit agreement of “I won’t cause problems for you, and you won’t cause problems for me.” The importance of maintaining polite long-term relationships within the community doesn’t apply to short-term renters, though, who’ll probably be gone in a few days’ time, and far too often ill-mannered minpaku guests party noisily late into the night, litter in the common-use areas of the buildings they stay in and on the surrounding streets, and otherwise.

Minpaku lodgings in Japan started off as a bit of a cottage industry, and the sector managed to build up significant momentum before widespread regulatory measures were put in place. Under the Private Lodging Business Law, minpaku are not allowed to accept guests for more than 180 nights in a calendar year, but many local municipalities have placed additional regulations on top of that. Most recently, Tokyo’s Kita Ward became the city’s 23rd ward to pass its own. As of January 7, Kita Ward will ban the opening of new minpaku in residential areas in which the homeowner is not present when guests are staying in the unit. Requiring the homeowner to be present should, theoretically, increase the minpaku operator’s connection, and personal responsibility, to the surrounding community, creating an accessible contact point for complaints from neighbors or regulatory enforcement by the ward, while discouraging management by remote companies whose facelessness makes it easier for them to ignore grievances.

▼ It’s harder for management to brush off complaints when they have to deal with them in-person.

Tokyo’s Taito Ward is also tightening restrictions on minpaku. As of October 1, no new minpaku within the ward will be allowed to accept guests on weekdays, and no new minpaku of any kind will be allowed to open in parts of the ward which are zoned for residential-use only. Taito is also taking action against four minpaku owners who collectively operate eight units within the ward. By law, minpaku operators are required to submit reports on a minpaku’s number of guests and nights in operation every two months, but the owners filed no reports at all for the eight properties for the period between December of 2025 and May of 2026. Taito is now giving the owners approximately three weeks to submit the required documents, and says that failure to do so will result in the owners’ names being publicly announced, followed by forced closures of the minpaku if the non-compliance continues.

Other parts of Tokyo are going even farther in their attempts to address residents’ growing irritation at minpaku. Shinjuku Ward, for example, is looking to add legislation that would not only designate areas within it as off-limits for new minpaku, but which would also force currently existing minpaku within them to shut down.

In total, Tokyo’s 23 central wards account for roughly 40 percent of all the minpaku in Japan, so it’s likely that other cities will be watching the effectiveness of these countermeasures very closely, and possibly basing their future policies on them in an effort to stave off resident complaints before any such friction with minpaku operators/guests occurs.

Source: Taito Ward (1, 2), Kita Ward, Asahi Shimbun, Tokyo MX, Mainichi Shimbun

title: Japanese viewers of Godzilla Minus Zero angered by unusual number of restroom goers
description: Godzilla films are famous for their subtlety and require complete concentration. Culture Day in Japan was on 3 November, and what better way to celebrate culture than by watching the latest Godzilla film, Godzilla Minus Zero? It was a thought held by many, as the monster movie drew in an amazing 910 million yen (US$5.8M) […]
content:
Godzilla films are famous for their subtlety and require complete concentration.

Culture Day in Japan was on 3 November, and what better way to celebrate culture than by watching the latest Godzilla film, Godzilla Minus Zero? It was a thought held by many, as the monster movie drew in an amazing 910 million yen (US$5.8M) on its opening day alone, breaking the record for a live-action film in Japan.

However, while the film itself has been incredibly well-received by critics and audiences alike, some moviegoers in Japan complained about their viewing experience. The biggest beef of all was that too many people were getting up to go to the restroom during the film.

One post by a social media user said they had an aisle seat during the movie and shortly into it, people had started going to the bathroom one after another, ruining their ability to get into the story. This might just sound like a single oversensitive reaction to this sort of thing, but the post generated significant discussion, with a majority of people agreeing.

Others also reported an inordinate number of people going to hit the head during their screenings of Godzilla Minus Zero (or Godzilla -0.0 as it’s known in Japan), including head counts they took during the film. It was enough to make me wonder if I was the weird one for paying absolutely no mind to other people going in and out of the theater in the many movies I’ve seen over the years.

There were a few comments to the contrary, saying that complaining about such a thing was going overboard. But there were many more people talking about how hard it was for them to fight the urge to pee towards the end of the movie, which, by the way, includes sitting through the entire credits. That is expected behavior among many moviegoers in Japan, not in the hopes of seeing additional scenes, but purely out of respect for the people who made the film.

I’d probably stop short of saying this is “Japanese culture” per se, but it definitely appears to be a prevailing sentiment here. To help get a sense of how people feel about this stuff, here’s a wide sampling of reactions to the situation, covering a range of opinions.

“When I saw it, no one went to the bathroom, but when the end credits started, a bunch of people got up right away to leave.”
“I think once that first person goes, everyone else feels like it’s okay, and the floodgates open.”
“I heard someone call the movie Godzilla vs King Ghidorah vs The Urge to Pee, lol.”
“A lot of people got up from their seats here too.”
“That’s the problem with blockbuster movies. They draw in people who don’t usually go to the movies.”
“When I saw it, the same people went in and out like six or seven times during the movie.”
“There was a crazy number of people going to the bathroom!”
“I was holding it in so long, it came out like a blast of atomic breath when I finally went.”
“Everyone had good manners when I saw it in Wakayama.”
“I saw two adults and one child get up during the movie, but no one got up during the credits.”
“You should just let it slide. Holding it in isn’t good for you.”
“That’s why I always watch on IMAX when possible. The screen is so big you can barely see anyone walking in front of it.”
“This is why I never go to movies. Some people might have medical issues, you know?”
“I get that it can’t be helped, but someone got up behind me, and I felt bad for all the people that person walked in front of.”
“Seriously? Calling people out just for using the restroom? I think etiquette is going in a weird direction.”
“I saw Street Fighter and had to go early on. I held it in right to the end of the credits, but it was really close.”
“Soooooo many people went to the restrooms. And during one of the scenes where a character laughed, some brat in the row behind me started laughing too. Shut the hell up!”
“Yeah, there were tons of people. I wonder why that is.”

Regardless of people’s feelings about the situation, the one objective observation here is that an inordinate number of people do seem to be going to the restroom during Godzilla Minus Zero specifically. It’s a bit of a lengthy movie, clocking in at 135 minutes, but some mention that the number of people ducking out for a moment well exceeded that of lengthier movies such as the 172-minute-long The Odyssey.

There were numerous theories as to why this is. One was that Godzilla, which dates back to the 1950s, tends to attract an older demographic who may lack the firm bladder control that the youth enjoys. The other is that the fact that a major commercial film opening on a public holiday brought in an inordinate number of people who weren’t “true movie buffs,” or perhaps just decided to see it in on a whim without planning their hydration accordingly.

By the way, according to many of the comments, a popular way to suppress the urge to urinate before watching a movie is to eat Bontan Ame candies or daifuku, the latter of which are little snacks made of sweet bean paste covered in mochi. There’s no science to back this up, but who am I to deny people their placebos?

There’s also a suspicion that a lot of people didn’t even leave to use a toilet. It could have been that some people weren’t prepared for the scenes of destruction depicted in the film, which can often resemble actual natural disasters and hit close to home for more than a few people in Japan.

Regardless of the cause, it seems the one thing we can learn from this is that when watching a movie in Japan, the safe bet is to sit perfectly still and quiet until the very last bit of footage hits the silver screen to avoid the silent wrath and judgmental stares of those around you.

title: America’s first-ever permanent One Piece store is now open [Photos]
description: The Straw Hat Pirates have dropped anchor in Los Angeles. Last month we got word that America would be getting its first-ever One Piece specialty store, and that the wait for it to open wouldn’t be very long. And while it was exciting for fans to look at the concept art for the One Piece […]
content:
The Straw Hat Pirates have dropped anchor in Los Angeles.

Last month we got word that America would be getting its first-ever One Piece specialty store, and that the wait for it to open wouldn’t be very long. And while it was exciting for fans to look at the concept art for the One Piece Mugiwara Store Los Angeles, now that the shop is actually open we can see what the real thing looks like!

November 6 was the grand opening date for the store, which is located at the Westfield Century City shopping center in Los Angeles. Representatives from One Piece animation rights holder Toei and Sony were on hand, as was Japanese professional soccer player Maya Yoshida, who has been playing for Major League Soccer’s Los Angeles Galaxy since 2023.

The real star power here though, of course, comes from the characters of the series, and there’s a three-meter (9.8-foot) tall statue of Luffy in his Gear 5 guise standing at the center of the shop, plus plenty of wanted posters of the Straw Hat Pirates posted inside, as shown by Yoshida here.

Chopper also gets a special “waverider Chopper” design just for the L.A. shop, showing him surfing the waters presumably just off the California coast.

Fittingly for fashion-conscious L.A., there are a lot of exclusive apparel items on offer…

…but this being a proper otaku-oriented retailer means that the shelves are also amply stocked with things such as figures and collected manga volumes too.

Coolest of all, the One Piece Mugiwara Store Los Angeles isn’t a limited-time, pop-up event, but a permanent place for fans to gather, just like the L.A. area’s recently opened Studio Ghibli specialty shop.

title: Japanese convenience store offering chance to have your shopping be effectively free for one day

Japan’s convenience stores have become world-famous, not only for their convenient locations and operating hours, but for their amazingly wide variety of genuinely tasty snacks, drinks, and even full meals. content:
Family Mart offering random reimbursements of up to 100,000 yen (US$630).

Japan’s convenience stores have become world-famous, not only for their convenient locations and operating hours, but for their amazingly wide variety of genuinely tasty snacks, drinks, and even full meals. Really, their only drawback is that they don’t always match the low prices you can find for similar items at supermarkets and drug stores.

There’s a potential upcoming exception to that at convenience store chain Family Mart, though, where if luck is on your side everything you buy in your shopping run could be effectively free.

On November 11, Family Mart customers who pay using the chain’s Fami Pay app can then play an in-app game, and if they win, they’ll be awarded Fami Pay credit equal to the entire cost of their purchases. The minimum purchase amount required to be eligible to pay is a paltry 111 yen (US$0.70), and the maximum possible prize is 100,000 yen. Technically, the 100,000-yen cap means that it’s possible you won’t be reimbursed for your entire purchase, but it’d be really, really hard to run up a bill greater than that in a single convenience store shopping trip.

There’s no need to be concerned about the sharpness of your gamer skills either, as the “game” you play consists entirely of pressing the green start button twice, then being informed of whether you’ve won or not.

Winners will immediately receive one yen worth of Fami Pay credit to confirm the win, and the rest of the credit will be added to your account in mid-December, with an expiration date of May 31. This delay is likely to prevent people from overspending and getting a bill they can’t afford to pay if they don’t win, since regardless of whether you win or not, you still need to be able to cover the cost of your bill at the time of purchase.

Eligibility to play the in-app game starts at midnight on November 11 and runs until 11:59 p.m. the same day, though the in-app game can be played anytime between November 11 and 13.

title: Starbucks Japan unveils new Potato Soupuccino that’s said to be more than just soup
description: New “self-care soup” blurs the line between soup and cappuccino. With temperatures starting to dip in Japan, Starbucks is adding warmth to its menu with an all-new Soupuccino. First introduced in 2025, the Soupuccino blurs the line between soup and cappuccino by adding a frothy, fluffy foam to the mix, creating a light and airy […]
content:
New “self-care soup” blurs the line between soup and cappuccino.

With temperatures starting to dip in Japan, Starbucks is adding warmth to its menu with an all-new Soupuccino. First introduced in 2025, the Soupuccino blurs the line between soup and cappuccino by adding a frothy, fluffy foam to the mix, creating a light and airy soup that looks great and is fun and easy to sip on.

▼ Now, after serving up the Soupuccino in truffle and pumpkin flavours, Starbucks is giving us an all-new flavour: Potato.

This new ingredient is said to add extra heartiness to the Soupuccino, with milk providing a gentle creaminess for a delicious “self-care soup”. The concept of “self-care” is one that the chain is actively using to promote the Soupuccino, with Starbucks saying it offers an opportunity for you to take care of yourself even during a busy day. Whether it’s a morning cup on a chilly day, a light snack during a work break, or a moment to unwind in the evening, Starbucks is encouraging customers to wrap both hands around the warm cup and enjoy “a gentle flavour encased in fluffy foam”.

The Potato Soupuccino is richly layered, replicating the fluffy, oven-baked texture and taste of potatoes as the main element. The first sip imparts the deep, savoury flavour of caramelised onions, followed by subtle hints of sweet vegetables. The gentle sweetness and buttery smoothness of potatoes brings everything together, creating a comforting flavour that’s perfect for the colder months.

▼ As you drink the soup, the flavours blend together, becoming even richer, while roasted almonds on top add crunch and a nutty accent.

Each cup is finished by a barista who steams the milk individually, giving the soup a smooth layer of foam, similar to a cappuccino, for a distinctive drinking experience. Another appealing feature is the option to pay a little extra to switch the milk to suit your personal tastes – switching to almond milk, for instance, complements the fragrant roasted almonds, further enhancing the taste and texture of the potato.

The Potato Soupuccino will be priced from 491 yen (US$3.11) for a Short and 530 yen for a Tall. According to Starbucks, the new release is more than just a soup – it’s a gesture of self-care that’s perfectly timed for the end of the year, when you may find yourself putting your own needs last as you get caught up in work, studies and household chores. The idea of taking a comforting break with a warm cup of soup in hand is one we can certainly get on board with, and we’ll definitely be trying it when it’s released for a limited time starting 13 November.

title: Katsuya takes perhaps a little too much liberty with its take on a Niigata soul food
description: We might be just a little bit saucy about this double-sauced version of a classic local specialty dish. Way back in 1931, a restaurant called Komatsu Parlor in Nagaoka, Niigata Prefecture served up a novel dish that was dubbed Western-style katsudon, in which tonkatsu (deep-fried pork cutlet) was placed on top of a bed of […]
content:
We might be just a little bit saucy about this double-sauced version of a classic local specialty dish.

Way back in 1931, a restaurant called Komatsu Parlor in Nagaoka, Niigata Prefecture served up a novel dish that was dubbed Western-style katsudon, in which tonkatsu (deep-fried pork cutlet) was placed on top of a bed of rice and topped with a thick, Western-style sauce, usually with either a ketchup or a demi-glace base. Not only was it tasty but it had an elegant, refined appearance, and it quickly became known as a popular “soul food” of the area.

Fast forward to the present, and modern tonkatsu and katsudon chain Katsuya released a limited-time menu item on November 6 for Aigake Western-Style Katsu Rice (869 yen/US$5.48). This dish is said to take inspiration from Nagaoka’s specialty dish while putting its own unique Katsuya spin on it…perhaps a little too much of a spin, in fact. Nevertheless, devoted fans of Katsuya that we are, we wanted to check it out for ourselves and headed to our local branch.

We were particularly curious about whether the sauce would be the ketchup type or demi-glace type. When our order arrived in front of us, we were a little bit shocked at the contents.

▼ It turns out that it had both.

The deep-fried pork loin was cut into six chunks, half of which were covered in a Japanese “aurora sauce” concoction of ketchup and Kewpie mayo…

…while the other half were drenched in a demi-glace sauce.

In other words, it was a best-of-both-worlds kind of deal. Some skeptics may think it’s unnecessary to combine both types on a single plate, but at least this way we could sample two different versions of the same dish.

The tonkatsu was resting on a small bed of white rice and on the side was also the typical accompaniment of shaved cabbage along with Japanese-style “Napolitan” ketchup spaghetti and a sunny-side-up fried egg. The plate as a whole looked a little bit busy, like a slightly chaotic fried food theme park.

We started our meal with the demi-glace side of the plate. It was strange how the addition of a sauce like this could elevate the ordinary tonkatsu into a somehow gourmet flavor.

On the other hand, while the aurora sauce on its own had a strong, sour kick–to the point where we tasted the same burst of acidity as with pickled ume–it evened out splendidly on top of the meat. This blended sauce might not be for everyone, but we actually preferred it to the demi-glace version.

Moving on, the pasta was springer than we initially thought and had that classic Napolitan taste with bits of bacon. Its flavor was further enhanced by its the seeping egg yolk neighbor.

There was also enough sauce beginning to pool on the plate that we were able to pour it over the cabbage and turn over a new leaf.

All in all, while we enjoyed the new Aigake Western-Style Katsu Rice dish, we have to wonder if all of Katsuya’s extreme modifications to its originator in Niigata are completely necessary. The plate also lacked a little bit of the visual impact of other recent Katsuya creations that we’ve tried. In any case, we’ll continue searching for more local takes on the tasty, deep-fried dish that have been around for decades.

title: Amazing Japanese yogurt spoon scoops up every last drop of dairy effortlessly
description: While the rest of the world is scraping away at their yogurt containers, we’re keeping things cultured with our new favorite spoon. In today’s installment of Japanese kitchen gadgets that just make everything easier, we’d like to present a spoon–not just any spoon, but a magical spoon that specializes in scooping up every last bit […]
content:
While the rest of the world is scraping away at their yogurt containers, we’re keeping things cultured with our new favorite spoon.

In today’s installment of Japanese kitchen gadgets that just make everything easier, we’d like to present a spoon–not just any spoon, but a magical spoon that specializes in scooping up every last bit of your yogurt.

OK, while we can’t guarantee that it’s actually imbued with magic, the spoon produced by Japanese houseware brand Marna sure seems to have some kind of mystical ability. We’d caught wind of it through the grapevine and decided to test it out for ourselves.

Its simple design involves a pliable tip made of silicone and a sturdy blue handle.

▼ We’ve got a good gut feeling about this one.

From a side view, it’s easy to see how the handle curves into an elegant angle at the tip.

Let’s test it out in action. Would it really make a difference in how we eat yogurt now and forevermore?

As we began eating, we noticed immediately how little effort it took to perfectly scour the inside of the container from all angles.

It felt like a mini spatula in this sense, also being quieter than a regular metal spoon.

Amazingly, there was almost no yogurt left clinging to the bottom or the sides of the cup once we had finished, despite not making any extra effort to scrape at the very end.

We next decided to hold a mini controlled experiment by eating one more of the exact same kind of yogurt using a regular metal spoon to compare the results.

We tried eating it as gracefully as possible but there was still some yogurt left at the bottom of the cup at the end. It seems that the fixed shape of the metal tip in this case prevented us from getting it all.

In conclusion, the spoon served its purpose incredibly well, living up to its promise of not wasting any yogurt with minimal effort.

▼ Yogurt container after using a regular metal spoon (left) and the special yogurt spoon (right)

In a fun collaboration, Marna also sells a version of the spoon together with Hiroshima-based company Chichiyasu, the first company in Japan to begin selling yogurt in 1917.

Marna’s yogurt spoon retails for 594 yen (US$3.75) and can be ordered through Marna’s official site or Rakuten Japan. While we never knew what we had been missing all of these years, it’s going to be hard to go back to eating yogurt any other way now. You might consider gifting one to yourself or to the yogurt fanatic in your life.

title: Pokémon card game’s expansion features art from Fist of the North Star creator
description: Tetsuo Hara shows he can draw for both blood-soaked martial arts action and Pokémon. The Pokémon Trading Card Game pumps out way too many cards for one single illustrator to handle all of them, and being approached by the Pokémon Company to draw one can be a major feather in the cap of upcoming artists […]
content:
Tetsuo Hara shows he can draw for both blood-soaked martial arts action and Pokémon.

The Pokémon Trading Card Game pumps out way too many cards for one single illustrator to handle all of them, and being approached by the Pokémon Company to draw one can be a major feather in the cap of upcoming artists with a talent for drawing cute and cuddly critters…but it turns out it can also be an appealing project for legendary veterans of drawing ultra-violent, extra-macho manga series too.

The game’s new Hado Seeker/Aura Seeker expansion packs (pictured above) are set to go on sale soon in Japan, and among the cards that could be waiting inside packs is one featuring Crasher Wake, the Pastoria City Gym Leader who first appeared in Pokémon Diamond and Pearl. The SAR (“special art rare”) version of the Crasher’s Passion card shows off an especially high level of detail on the character’s muscles, which makes sense once you know that it was drawn by none other than Tetsuo Hara, creator and artist of Fist of the North Star!

Hara, who began drawing his post-apocalyptic marital arts saga in 1983, brings his distinct aesthetic of heavy shadowing to convey the mass of characters’ muscles, plus a whole lot of fist-shaped after images to represent rapid punch flurries, to the artwork. “Crasher is a pro wrestler, so I thought a lot about how best to show his toughness and physique,” the artist says. “I always want to pursue a sense of realism in my artwork, so I have to take into consideration how stylized I can get. At first, I was planning to draw Crashed with even bigger muscles, but after considering how that would or wouldn’t align with fans’ perception of the character, I ended up toning it down.”

For the illustration’s layout, Hara says he wanted Crasher to be up in a wrestling ring, in order to create a powerful presence, but drawing him from that angle ran the risk of making his face look tiny, so he decided to have the character angled to be looking down from on high. This also allowed him to add in a few of the ring’s overhead lights in a stealthy homage to the constellation-motif that appears in Fist of the North Star. Hara also says that once he started adding after-images of Crasher’s punches, he realized the composition needed more and more, so many that he found himself thinking “Maybe I shouldn’t have done this” because of all the extra work he’d created for himself, but in the end it seems like a pretty safe bet that most fans are going to be very satisfied with how things turned out. For those wanting a closer look, the original artwork for the card will be on display at the Pokémon Card Station specialty shop attached to the Pokémon Center Ikebukuro store in Tokyo from November 30 to January 11.

This actually isn’t Hara’s first time to lend his talents to the Pokémon Trading Card Game. In 2024, he drew artwork for a special Palafin card that was part of the Terastal Fest Ex, which also featured an homage to Fist of the North Star protagonist Kenshiro’s iconic Hundred Crack Fist attack.

Hara says that there’s a unique challenge in balancing his personal artistic sensibilities with the atmosphere of the Pokémon world, but that he’s enjoyed finding a way to blend the two, and the experience he acquired working on the Palafin card made the process of creating the Crasher one smoother, so hopefully there’ll be more Pokémon projects for him in the future. For the time being, though, the Hado Seeker expansion packs are scheduled to go on sale in Japan on November 27.

description: Meowgaroo Hoodie 3’s clever design points mean you don’t have to choose between playing with your cat and playing your games. content:
Meowgaroo Hoodie 3’s clever design points mean you don’t have to choose between playing with your cat and playing your games.

As the temperature gets lower and days get shorter, you might be thinking it’s time to bundle up and hunker down for the winter with warm clothing and fun games. Really, though, it’s time to bundle up and game on while simultaneously abiding by your cat’s whims.

Thankfully, Japan’s Bibilab is conscious of the big-picture situation, and is prepared to offer a holistic solution with its newest creation, the Meowgaroo Hoodie 3.

Also known as the Nyangaru Parka 3 (nyan being the Japanese equivalent of “meow” and “parka” being the more common way to refer to hoodies in Japan), the Meowgaroo Hoodie 3, as its name implies, is the latest generation of Bibilab’s cat-conscious roomwear line.

Since cats are notoriously averse to compromising, the designers realize that when your feline friend wants to snuggle, there’s no way to dissuade it of the notion, and so the hoodie has a large marsupial-inspired pouch on the stomach for your cat to crawl inside of, keeping it cozily close and supported while keeping your hands free to work a game controller or keyboard/mouse setup.

That’s far from the garment’s only clever design point, though. The decorative cat ears on the hood also stand out right away, but what you might miss at first glance is that the tips of the drawstring cords…

…are actually fuzzy cat teasers, meaning that the hoodie has built-in cat toys, letting you quickly transition from playing games to playing with your cat without even having to get up from your seat.

▼ This is much better than staring at the “Please wait – online matchmaking in progress” screen.

It also might not be immediately apparent why the Meowgaroo Hoodie 3 has such a spaciously sized chest pocket, given that chest pockets themselves are rare on sweatshirts. The reason is that it’s designed to be big enough to hold your smartphone…

…so that you can record cute, candid videos of your cat while it’s in the pouch.

Getting back to the pouch, it also has a drawstring that allows you to adjust the dimensions to keep your kitty as snugly secure as needed. Of course, as a space for your pet to cuddle, play, and possible snooze, the pouch is going to end up with cat hair inside it, but even that has been taken into account by the designers, who opted for a dual-layer construction that lets you unsnap and remove the lining for easier cleaning/washing.

Bibilab is the same company who, back in the spring, created an entire work-from-home (or game-from-home) desk designed around the idea that your cat has no qualms about encroaching on your personal space, and the company says the Meowgaroo Hoodie 3 is part of its continuing efforts to transform the feeling of being harassed by your cat into an enjoyable time for pet and human alike.

▼ The integrated solution of Meowgaroo Hoodie 3 with Bibilab’s Neko House Desk and Cat tower Rack

The Meowgaroo Hoodie 3 is available in medium and large sizes, and can be ordered for 8,900 yen (US$56) through Amazon Japan here.

title: Kenshi Yonezu’s Lemon hits 1 billion views on YouTube and he’s still not quite sure why
description: He handed life a ‘Lemon.’ Back in 2018, one song in particular was tearing up the charts in Japan. It was a somewhat somber pop song balanced with an energetic rock rhythm, known as ‘Lemon.’ It won several awards, was played on calculators, and in addition to charting number one on the Billboard Japan Hot […]
content:
He handed life a ‘Lemon.’

Back in 2018, one song in particular was tearing up the charts in Japan. It was a somewhat somber pop song balanced with an energetic rock rhythm, known as ‘Lemon.’ It won several awards, was played on calculators, and in addition to charting number one on the Billboard Japan Hot 100 for 2018, it has continued to chart in the annual Hot 100 every year since.

Now, eight years since its initial release, the song has earned yet another honor by surpassing one billion views on YouTube. It’s rarefied air that ‘Lemon’ now shares with the likes of ‘Baby Shark,’ and in honor of this achievement, songwriter Kenshi Yonezu released the following statement, translated from Japanese:

“In all honesty, I still don’t really get why ‘Lemon’ became such a huge song with this wide a reach. I mean, of course I never set out to make a trivial piece of music, and I totally get that Lemon only grew into a phenomenon because it was the theme song for the truly excellent television show Unnatural, and because the production team treated it with the utmost care and affection.

But I remember back when I first released Lemon, I was completely blown away by the explosive momentum its reputation spread with. I thought to myself, ‘Hang on… Is this really going to be my signature song?’ It was like lighting a small scrap of wood on fire, thinking I’d start a campfire, only to have the flames spread instantly and eventually turn into a full-blown wildfire with me just standing there holding a lighter in one hand and a bucket of water in the other. That’s how the whole situation looked from my perspective.

When I was growing up, I’d see these brilliant musicians act dismissive about their own signature songs, claiming they never saw what was so good about them or refusing to play them live because they didn’t like them. At the time, I’d think to myself, ‘It’s clearly a great song! Don’t play cool and act like you don’t know it!’ But now that it’s happened to me, I finally understand why they felt the way they did.

To put it simply, songs like this end up leaving the creator’s original intentions and personal feelings in the dust. They move at such an incredible speed they basically become public domain overnight. I guess it’s only natural to resent that a little bit. In a way, ‘Lemon’ has allowed me to pull up a chair at the same table as these great musicians, at least in the sense that I can empathize with them now.

It might sound like I’m complaining, but I want to be clear that I have always felt and always will feel tremendous gratitude towards ‘Lemon.’ It took an untamed, raggedy stray dog from the sticks like me and threw my life into complete chaos. It showed me sights that I’d never dream of seeing and guided me into a life so absurdly entertaining that it nearly wears me out.

Some nights I imagine myself in the future as a pathetic and withered old man singing ‘Lemon’ and strumming along in front of some kids 40 years younger than me. They’d bluntly tell me off, saying, ‘Give all those depressing songs a break,’ and ‘No one even remembers that song anymore,’ but that’s just the way it is.”

It’s good to see the fame hasn’t changed Yonezu much. He still seems to be the somewhat brooding but incredibly insightful guy he was eight years ago. Online comments were also intrigued by his surprisingly astute and sincere reflections on having a billion-view song.

“What a wonderful statement that really conveys Yonezu’s true feelings and sense of astonishment about this.”
“Wow! Last time I checked, it was about 600 million.”
“He’s totally talking about Bump of Chicken and ‘Tentai Kansoku’ in that middle part, lol!”
“He’s really got class. You can see how he struggles to process how the public reaction doesn’t align with his own assessment of his work without sounding bitter about it.”
“He’s an artist, musician, and a great writer too.”
“That comment makes me happy! Congratulations on ‘Lemon’ hitting a billion views!”
“It’s the classic story. The things an artist doesn’t try too hard to make end up being the most highly regarded.”
“What an annoyingly long-winded rant. I read the whole thing, but still…”
“He should try writing an autobiography sometime. I’d like to read it.”
“I like the way he writes about ‘Lemon’ better than ‘Lemon.’”

I kind of agree that ‘Lemon’ isn’t even really Yonezu firing on all cylinders, and would argue he’s done some stuff much more deserving of a billion views. However, the part about him feeling bad when people misunderstand his work is really making me nervous about our 1,000-word analysis of how ‘Paprika’ is really about children who died. He’s never copped to it, but I’d eat my hat if it isn’t.

title: New Era celebrates three decades of Pokémon with new 30th anniversary cap line [Photos]

content:
Every Pokémon Trainer needs a hat, right?

Over his multiple decades as the protagonist of the Pokémon anime, Satoshi/Ash taught fans many things. The importance of believing in yourself. The power of friendship. And, of course, that no matter where your journeys in life may take you, a good hat is always nice to have.

The first two of those are things that you can only achieve through personal courage and life experience, but the third is something that New Era is ready to provide, through its new Pokémon collaboration line.

Part of the ongoing celebration of the Pokémon franchise’s 30th anniversary, New Era has crafted a collection featuring an all-star cast of creatures. One of the most eye-catching, from any angle, is the 59 Fifty Pokémon 30 All Over cap, with Pikachu on the front and Venusaur, Charizard, and Blastoise covering the other sides.

The original starter trio show up in their pre-evolution forms too, with Bulbasaur, Charmander, and Squirtle, plus Pikachu too, printed all across the cap’s lining.

If that’s too busy for your tastes, this 59 Fifty has them hanging out together on the front, with the 30th anniversary emblem on the right side and the Pokémon logo on the back.

Meanwhile, Mew’s intimidating presence means that he has the front of his 59 Fifty all to himself.

Moving on to more abstract expressions of Pokémon, the Pikachu 9 Forty A-frame Trucker caps render the series mascot in rhinestones, with your choice of three different color schemes.

And for those looking for a more understated style, New Era has a whole slew of 9 Twenty caps for fans of Pikachu, Eevee, Ditto, Mewtwo, and the Gen-1 starters.

▼ Mewtwo’s heart-shaped tail pose is an especially charming touch.

Prices range from 4,950 yen (US$31) for the 9 Twenty caps to 5,500 for the 9 Forty and 7,700 for the 59 Fifty models. The lineup goes on sale November 20 at New Era stores in Japan and through the New Era online shop here.

title: Two Tokyo neighborhoods to gather on bridge and shift their recognized border through tug-of-war
description: Sibling ward rivalry doesn’t need solid ground for its bragging-rights battlefield. My parents were very strict about the Baseel brothers not fighting with each other while we were growing up, but I’ve been told that it’s not unusual for siblings to squabble. And so it is that Tokyo’s Sumida and Taito Wards, neighbors who have […]
content:
Sibling ward rivalry doesn’t need solid ground for its bragging-rights battlefield.

My parents were very strict about the Baseel brothers not fighting with each other while we were growing up, but I’ve been told that it’s not unusual for siblings to squabble. And so it is that Tokyo’s Sumida and Taito Wards, neighbors who have been sister wards since 1977, have begun meeting every year and attempting to expand their territory at the other’s expense by shifting the symbolic borderline between the two.

Fittingly, the two parties want this annual contest to take place on their border, but that presents a bit of a problem, since flowing between Sumida and Taito is the Sumida River. They’ve managed to work out a solution, though, and so later this month the Sakurabashi Bridge will once again become the scene of the Sumida River Tug-of-War Tournament.

The exact mid-point of the bridge is one of the very few publicly accessible points along the wards’ borderline, and the only one exclusively for pedestrian crossings. So since 2024, Sumida and Taito have been sending teams of representatives for a series of tug-of-war battles to be waged on Sakurabashi, with the agreement that both wards will recognize that the border has been moved by one meter (3.3 feet) in the direction of the losing ward, giving the winner that much larger of a domain.

▼ Video of the 2025 Sumida River Tug-of-War Tournament

For the last two years, Taito has won the tournament, as documented in this illustration showing the border in 2023 (yellow line), 2024 (dotted red line), and 2025 (solid red line)

▼ The Sakurabashi Bridge, with the Tokyo Skytree standing tall on the Sumida Ward side of the river

It should be noted that while Tokyo’s wards do each have some level of autonomy, the municipal-level administration doesn’t actually let its component parts go around redrawing their boundaries, and so the territorial prize at stake in the Sumida River Tug-of-War Tournament is really a symbolic one (this is also why the tournament is followed by a friendly celebration at a riverside terrace). The length of the bridge also means that neither ward is likely to reach the opposite riverbank, barring some sort of highly localized protein deficiency that leaves one group of residents significantly weaker than the other for several decades. Nevertheless, there’s civic pride at stake, and Sumida is no doubt eager to avenge its two consecutive losses.

Rather than recruiting entire teams, participants apply to their ward individually, with organizers assembling 12 teams, including two children’s teams, of 10 members each from the pool. On the day of the tournament, opposing teams will compete in a best-two-out-of-three format, and in order to prevent a 6-6 tie, each ward also puts together an all-star team, made up of members of its 12 others, for a 13th match.

This year’s Sumida River Tug-of-War Tournament is scheduled to start at 10:30 a.m. on November 15 atop the Sakurabashi Bridge, which is roughly a 15-minute walk from Asakusa Station in Taito Ward or Oshiage Station in Sumida Ward. It’ll also be the first year for the broadcasting club of Taito’s Iwakura High School to be on-site providing live color commentary, which should give the whole event some good “crazy anime series sports episode” energy.

▼ Sakurabashi Bridge

As of this writing, Sumida Ward is still accepting applicants through the event’s official website, but even if you’re not pulling, spectators are welcome to come out and cheer one, or both, of the sides on, with no admission tickets required.

It’s like a skating party in your bathroom, and all your Sanrio friends are invited.

Part of the secret to the enduring popularity of Hello Kitty and her Sanrio pals is what loyal friends they are. Sure, you could take the cynical interpretation that their incredibly wide variety of character merch is simply a way to multiply revenue streams, but there’s no denying that it also means that almost no matter what you’re doing in life, there’s a way for you to do it with your favorite Sanrio characters keeping you company…even in the bathroom.

This week, Fukuoka-based paper products company Marutomi Seishi began selling its newest collaboration with Sanrio, the “Sanrio Winter 12-Roll Double.” And yes, that’s “double” as in “double-ply toilet paper.” This isn’t just a case of playful packaging, either, the paper itself is covered in illustrations.

▼ It’s only fitting that Sanrio toilet paper be as kind and gentle as the characters that appear on it.

Over a dozen Sanrio characters are featured, including Helloy Kitty, Pompompurin, Cinnamoroll, My Melody, Kuromi, Pochacco, and Hangyodon, on two patterns.

The new paper has a wintery motif, depicting the Sanrio friends bundled up for an ice skating outing rendered in a cool snowy color scheme.

Marutomi Seishi also promises that the Sanrio toiler paper has a “sweets fragrance.” That’s not to be confused with a generic “sweet” smell, but instead appears to indicate that this toilet paper has the aroma of some sort of dessert.

The goal, Marutomi Seishi says, is for the Sanrio toilet paper to “create a peaceful, tranquil atmosphere in your bathroom,” and the 12-roll pack should be showing up now in Japanese drugstores and other housewares retailers.

title: Cinnabon gets into the Japanese spirit with new Wagokorobon treats
description: Cinnabon Japan finds two new ways to mix its own dessert traditions with Japan’s. content:
Cinnabon Japan finds two new ways to mix its own dessert traditions with Japan’s.

Unlike some other American sweets suppliers who’ve set up shop in Japan, Cinnabon doesn’t have Japan-exclusive menu items all that often. We can probably chalk that up to the chain’s key ingredient, cinnamon, being a distinct flavor that doesn’t feature very often at all in traditional Japanese desserts. Leave the cinnamon in, and it’s hard to find a cordial combo with Japanese ingredients, but take it out, and it’s not really a cinnamon bun anymore, is it?

But every now and again Cinnabon Japan does find a way to create new desserts with Japanese inspirations, and it’s got two on its menu right now.

Collectively called the Wagokorobon line (wagokoro meaning “Japanese heart”), the first of the two items is the Kuri (Chestnut) Matcha Mini Chocobon. This starts as one of Cinnabon’s cinnamon-light Chocobons, which get chocolate kneaded into the standard Cinnabon dough plus a drizzle of chocolate sauce. This Wagokorobon version also gets a chestnut frosting, representing one of Japan’s favorite fall dessert flavors, plus a whole lot of matcha sprinkled on top. There’s so much green tea that it looks like it’ll definitely impart a noticeable texture, but that powdery sensation shouldn’t be too far off from the sprinkled cinnamon on conventional cinnamon buns.

Meanwhile, there’s a different granular guest star on the Kuromitsu Kinako Minibon: kinako, or roasted soybean powder. While not as sweet as the sweet red bean paste called anko that often shows up in Japanese confectioneries, kinako is noticeably sweet and fragrant, with a slight nutty quality to its flavor. Kinako’s texture is fine enough that it can make the things it’s sprinkled on feel a little dry, though, so it’s often accompanied by kuromitsu, a kind of Japanese brown sugar molasses, as it is here, and the mix of sweet, sticky, powdery sensations should slot very nicely into what you’d want from a cinnamon bun while still having an unmistakably Japanese taste.

Both Wagokorobon items are on sale at Cinnabon Japan branches now, and are scheduled to be available until late November.

title: Japan’s new matcha vending machines serve freshly prepared matcha in five different strengths
description: Enjoy the taste of freshly whisked matcha at the touch of a button. Japan is home to many different types of vending machines, and some of the most impressive are the ones that serve freshly ground coffee, with the beans ground and each cup brewed to order inside the machine. content:
Enjoy the taste of freshly whisked matcha at the touch of a button.

Japan is home to many different types of vending machines, and some of the most impressive are the ones that serve freshly ground coffee, with the beans ground and each cup brewed to order inside the machine. The process is even shown live on a monitor, so customers can watch their coffee being prepared.

Now, Toyo Vending, the company behind the popular Mill-Ground Coffee vending machines, has teamed up with tea giant Ito En to bring this technology to powdered green tea. The result is “Japan Quality Matcha”, a new style of drink that uses carefully selected matcha ingredients and specialised preparation technology to deliver an authentic taste similar to freshly whisked matcha, with five different strengths to choose from.

The new machines aim to cater to the growing demand for matcha, making it even more accessible and convenient, particularly for overseas visitors. Unlike regular drink vending machines, which are filled with bottles and cans, these ones prepare drinks to order, with the process beginning only after the customer presses the button. The company says its technology produces a taste similar to freshly whisked matcha, while also allowing customers to choose how strong they want their drink.

The machines are easy to spot, with three different all-green designs, each of which takes its inspiration from Japanese scenery and traditional culture. The first design features a deep green colour inspired by Japanese landscapes, designed to evoke a sense of tranquillity and relaxation.

The second features traditional Japanese patterns, while the third, described as “Modern Luxury”, combines a large display screen with an image of matcha against a premium tea plantation. The machines are set to be located at high-traffic locations like expressway rest areas, train stations, airports, commercial facilities, and tourist destinations popular with international visitors.

These machines are an exciting new way to enjoy matcha, and are already beginning to generate a lot of buzz in Japan. Their uniqueness has been summed up by Toyo Vending CEO Yoshimasa Wakamatsu, who has this message for matcha fans.

“We have always been committed to providing an uncompromising cup of coffee through our Mill-Ground Coffee machines, and now we’ve applied that same technology to matcha, one of Japan’s traditional treasures. We’re delighted to have found such an excellent partner in Ito En and to be able to deliver authentic Japan Quality to customers both in Japan and overseas. Through the familiarity of vending machines, we hope to offer a new way to experience matcha.”

We certainly can’t wait to try the new matcha, and all five different strengths that allow you to select your preferred intensity, when they begin appearing around Japan this month. With a variety of options to choose from, including regular matcha and matcha lattes, these look set to become the next hot trend to flood your socials, so keep an eye out for them during your travels.

title: Restaurant opens in Japan with all-dementia waitresses, serves up ramen, awareness, and kindness
description: Restaurant of Mistaken Orders is upfront about potential problems in order to cultivate future understanding. Japan has incredibly high customer service standards, especially where restaurants are concerned. Because of that, a restaurant saying, in advance, that it might get your order wrong seems like a recipe for dissatisfied diners, but that strategy led to smiles […]
content:
Restaurant of Mistaken Orders is upfront about potential problems in order to cultivate future understanding.

Japan has incredibly high customer service standards, especially where restaurants are concerned. Because of that, a restaurant saying, in advance, that it might get your order wrong seems like a recipe for dissatisfied diners, but that strategy led to smiles all around, plus a few appreciative tears, recently in the city of Matsuyama, Ehime Prefecture.

“Restaurant of Mistaken Orders” didn’t get its unusual name through a translation error, as that really is a pretty accurate rendering of its Japanese name, Chumon wo Machigaeru Kamoshirenai Ryori-ten. That less-than-perfect precision isn’t due to a lack of effort or concern on the restaurant’s part, though, but because the waitstaff is composed of senior citizens with dementia.

Restaurant of Mistaken Orders, which started out in 2018, operates on a popup basis, partnering with preexisting restaurants which serve as a venue for the unique eatery for the day. For its most recent iteration in Matsuyama, Restaurant of Mistaken Orders teamed up with Tenryu Ramen on September 21, which was both the Japanese public holiday Respect for the Aged Day and World Alzheimer’s Day.

▼ Restaurant of Mistaken Orders at Tenryu Ramen

It should be pointed out that the driving philosophy behind Restaurant of Mistaken Orders is not “Let’s get those dementia-stricken seniors working!” Instead, the purpose of the venture is to foster a greater sense of awareness and consideration towards people living with dementia, and also to give the participating seniors a sense of confidence and accomplishment by showing that their condition doesn’t have to mean complete debilitation and isolation from human interaction. “We hope this feeling of openness and understanding will spread across Japan, and through the world” says the organization in is mission statement, showing that the restaurant setting is meant to serve as a sort of metaphor for kindness wherever one may encounter someone with dementia.

In Matsuyama, four local seniors, ranging in age from 78 to 88, took orders and served diners, including the daughter and granddaughter of one of the participants (the daughter is the woman who can be seen wiping away tears in the above video, while talking about how emotionally moving it is to see her mother staying active). “If we took our time and listened and spoke patiently, we could understand each other,” says a father of a family of four that are at Restaurant of Mistaken Orders of communicating with the staff, and one of the elderly waitresses, at the end of the event, said with a smile “I was really happy to get to see so many people and talk with them.”

▼ The project’s concept video

With community outreach and public awareness being the primary goals, operating profits aren’t really a priority for Restaurant of Mistaken Orders, and the organization accepts online donations here for those that aren’t able to come in for a bite to eat, but still want to lend a helping hand.

title: Get the taste of the U.K. in Tokyo with 99 Flakes, meat pies, and Jaffa Cakes
description: This tiny Shibuya spot brings quintessential UK snacks straight to central Tokyo. Whether you have moved to a different country and pining for the foodstuffs of the motherland or you are interested in foreign cuisine without the hefty price tag of the airfare, specialty import stores are a treat to walk around. Tucked away amid […]
content:
This tiny Shibuya spot brings quintessential UK snacks straight to central Tokyo.

Whether you have moved to a different country and pining for the foodstuffs of the motherland or you are interested in foreign cuisine without the hefty price tag of the airfare, specialty import stores are a treat to walk around. Tucked away amid the towering buildings of Shibuya, you’ll find The British Shop, a grocery store specializing in British ingredients with its own eat-in area.

Located just outside exit B3 of the Shibuya subway station, The British Shop’s footprint is even smaller than a convenience store, but the shelves are lined with British foods and a table is set up in the center from which you can enjoy a variety of foods.

One of the highlights for a nostalgic Brit would be the ice cream van staple of a 99 Flake, essentially a soft-serve ice cream cone with a Cadbury’s Flake chocolate bar inserted into it.

Unfortunately, sales were suspended on the day we visited, but we still got to enjoy some chocolatey goodness with our ice cream.

To satisfy our ice cream cravings, we opted for a double scoop (750 yen [US$4.74]) along with a Flake (100 yen): the first scoop was vanilla and clotted cream, and the second blackcurrant and double cream.

While clotted cream is an indispensable accompaniment to scones, it has to be said that seeing it as an ice cream flavor is pretty unusual. The taste was unexpectedly light with a gentle sweetness, reproducing the lightness of actual clotted cream. Combining a subtly milky taste with the rich aroma of vanilla made for an addictive, delicious flavor.

Blackcurrant is known as ‘cassis’ in Japan, where it is arguably seen most as a part of alcoholic drinks, but in the UK it is much more widely enjoyed in squashes (fruit cordials) or as a component to desserts. The tartness of the ice cream wasn’t too strong, and had a taste that made us keep coming back in for another scoop.

After spending any amount of time in Japan, you come to realize that ‘pies’ are almost always of the dessert variety, often containing fruits, but at this little shop you can purchase the Chunky Beef Pie for 600 yen, which is made with huge chunks of diced beef and has a very rich taste.

After coming all the way to the store, it would be unthinkable if you left without picking up some snacks as a souvenir, and what better way to do that than to take home the subject of Britain’s biggest snack debate: the Jaffa Cake (520 yen).

Delectable treats made by layering a soft sponge cake with a sweet-and-sour orange filling and coating it with chocolate, these once featured as the main focus in a legal case to determine whether they were actually biscuits (cookies) or, indeed as the name would suggest, cakes. Spoiler: they’re cakes. Since Jaffa Cakes are hard to find in Japan, these are a must-grab item if you visit the shop, and being sweet they make a perfect accompaniment to a cup of tea.

Next up were the Somerset Cheddar and Shallot flavor Savoursmiths crisps.

A high-end crisp brand from the UK comes at a price of 220 yen for a bag, which is definitely on the higher side when comparing other potato chips in a Japanese supermarket. The crunchy texture was exquisite, and we ended up finishing them before we had even realized it.

Sometimes a trip to Tokyo is not easy, so there’s also the option of ordering from the shop online, where shipping is free on orders over 12,000 yen.

The British Shop offers everything from classic snacks to slightly niche ingredients, with items such as bacon, bread, seasonings, and Yorkshire Tea Gold all available to purchase.  If you’re not as unlucky as us when visiting the store, you’ll also get to try the quintessential British summertime treat of a 99 Flake all the way on the other side of the globe.
